# Dimension 1: Architecture Trade-offs

Source details: [../citations.md](../citations.md)

---

## 1. The Pendulum Swing: Industry Consensus Shifting

The 2020s have seen a notable shift in industry consensus away from microservices-by-default toward monolith-first approaches. Key voices driving this shift:

- **Martin Fowler** (2015): "Don't even consider microservices unless you have a system that's too complex to manage as a monolith" [1]. Microservices incur a "MicroservicePremium" that is only justified for complex systems [2].
- **Kelsey Hightower** (Google Cloud): "Monoliths are the future because the problem people are trying to solve with microservices doesn't really line up with reality" [3]. "If people would just start with organized modular code, we can make the deployment architecture an implementation detail" [3].
- **DHH** (Rails creator, October 2025): "The majestic monolith remains undefeated for the vast majority of web apps. Replacing method calls with network calls makes everything harder, slower, and more brittle. It should be the absolute last resort" [4].
- **Sam Newman** (author of "Building Microservices"): "Microservices are not a good choice for most startups" [7]. Most companies would do better with "the highly underrated option of a modular monolith" [8].
- **Chris Richardson** (microservices.io): Principle #1 for refactoring to microservices: "Don't" [136]. "Monolith is not actually an anti-pattern" [136].

## 2. Quantified Performance and Cost Data

### Microservices Overhead

| Metric | Value | Context | Source |
|--------|-------|---------|--------|
| Core reduction (microservices to monolith) | 78 cores to 9 cores | Google HotOS'23, 11 services at 10K qps | [23] |
| Latency reduction | 15x (median 0.38ms) | Same Google study | [23] |
| Cost savings | 10x | Same Google study | [23] |
| Service mesh latency overhead (worst case) | Up to 166% (Istio at 3200 RPS) | arXiv mTLS study | [17] |
| Istio latency increase at 3200 RPS | 166% | arXiv mTLS study | [17] |
| Service mesh vCPU overhead | Up to 163% more cores | arXiv mTLS study | [17] |
| Operational cost multiplier | ~3x | Industry reports | [27] |
| Infrastructure cost multiplier | 3.75x-6x | Derived from reversal case studies | [9] [102] |

### Reversal Case Studies

| Company | What Happened | Result | Source |
|---------|---------------|--------|--------|
| Amazon Prime Video | Step Functions + S3 architecture hit scaling limit at 5% of expected load | 90% infrastructure cost reduction | [9] [10] |
| Twilio Segment | 140+ services, 3-person team, velocity plummeted, defect rate exploded | Consolidated to single "Centrifuge" service; 46 library improvements in 6 months vs 32 in all of 2016 | [12] |
| Istio | Pilot, Galley, Citadel, Mixer as separate microservices | Consolidated to single `istiod` binary; internal modularity preserved | [130] |
| Grape Up client | 25 microservices for a small application | Consolidated to 5 services; 82% infra cost reduction, 70% monitoring cost drop | [102] |

### Key Nuances

Adrian Cockcroft (former VP Cloud Architecture, AWS) on Prime Video: "This definitely isn't a microservices-to-monolith story. It's a Step Functions-to-microservices story" [11]. Werner Vogels (Amazon CTO): "Building evolvable software systems is a strategy, not a religion" [10].

## 3. Shopify: The 2.8M LOC Monolith at Scale

Shopify Core is the canonical example of a monolith operating at extreme scale [13] [14]:

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| Lines of code | 2.8 million |
| Commits | 500,000 |
| Active developers | 1,000+ |
| Black Friday GMV | $5 billion |
| Peak requests/minute | 284 million |
| Total requests in 24 hours | 173 billion |
| Peak DB queries/second | 45 million |

Shopify uses **Packwerk** (open-source Ruby gem) to enforce module boundaries at build time [13]. Scaling is handled via **Pods** — isolated database clusters sharded by `shop_id`, routed by "Sorting Hat" [14]. Certain components (payment processing, user identity) are extracted only when "specific demands around scale, security, or isolation make it necessary" [13].

## 4. Team Size Decision Framework

Multiple independent sources converge on similar thresholds [21] [22]:

| Team Size | Recommended Architecture | Rationale |
|-----------|------------------------|-----------|
| 1-10 developers | Monolith | Microservices overhead slows you down |
| 10-50 developers | Modular monolith | Structure without distribution complexity |
| 50+ developers | Microservices become beneficial | Coordination costs justify the investment |

Key claim: "Microservices require 3 to 5 developers per service to maintain properly. A 15-person team managing 12 services isn't being agile; they're drowning" [21].

**Primary signal for decomposition** (Sam Newman): delivery contention — "they have lots of developers working on a given problem, and those developers are getting in each other's way" [7].

## 5. The Counterargument: Stefan Tilkov

Published on Fowler's own site as a direct rebuttal [119] [25]:

- "I'm firmly convinced that starting with a monolith is usually exactly the wrong thing to do" [119].
- "If you are actually able to build a well-structured monolith, you probably don't need microservices in the first place" [119].
- "A monolith won't magically contain services waiting to be liberated" [119].
- Proposed **Self-Contained Systems** (SCS) as a middle ground — autonomous services larger than microservices but responsible for one business domain [119].

## 6. The Microservice Premium

Martin Fowler defined the concept: "Microservices impose a cost on productivity that can only be made up for in more complex systems" [26]. This includes:

- Network overhead: method calls (microseconds, deterministic) become network requests (milliseconds, probabilistic) [28]
- Reliability degradation: "One 99.9% reliable service becomes 99% reliable when called ten times" [28]
- Infrastructure prerequisites: on-demand deployment environments, independent CI/CD, distributed security/debugging/monitoring [24]
- Team structure alignment: "Decompose services to match team boundaries, not the other way around" [28]

## Gaps and Limitations

1. **Team size thresholds** (1-10, 10-50, 50+) represent industry heuristics from blog posts, not empirical research [21] [22]. No rigorous study has validated these boundaries.
2. **"3x operational cost"** claim lacks a traceable primary study [27].
3. **Infrastructure cost multiplier** (3.75x-6x) is derived by inference from reversal case studies, not measured directly.
4. **Survivorship bias**: Published reversal stories are disproportionately from high-profile companies. The population of quiet failures or quiet successes is unknown.
5. **Shopify's scale data** is from first-party engineering blogs [13] [14], which are authoritative but naturally present the positive case.
6. The **Tilkov counterargument** [119] remains largely theoretical — few published case studies demonstrate the SCS approach at scale.
